about: The lesson benchmark's concept vocabulary: what a coach would name as the idea behind a move. Built from the dev annotators' free-text concepts, grouped into families. A concept that fits none is mapped to "other".

families.material: Loose pieces and counting: what can be taken, and whether it's really defended
families.tempo: Time: development and moves that gain or lose it
families.pieces: Where pieces stand and which squares and lines they use

concepts.means: Left a piece or pawn undefended where it can be taken for nothing, including by moving it or by pushing a pawn to an unprotected square.
Attackers against defenders: moving to, capturing on or pushing into a square attacked more times than it is defended, or capturing a pawn that is defended.
examples: capturing a defended pawn with the queen
e3 pawn attacked twice, defended once

concepts.means: Missed a piece or pawn the opponent left loose that could simply be taken.
examples: missed a free pawn on d4

concepts.means: The move took away, traded off or moved away a piece that was defending something, which then falls.
Something looks defended but the defender can't recapture: it is pinned, overloaded or tied to another job.
examples: d4 pawn defended by a pinned pawn
pawn defender tied to the rook

concepts.means: Took material at the cost of development, king safety or coordination, and the opponent's activity outweighs it.
examples: pawn grab with back rank weak

concepts.means: One piece or pawn attacks two targets at once (knight, pawn, queen or other fork), whether walked into or missed.
A piece can't move (or can't move safely) because something more valuable is behind it on the line.
A valuable piece is attacked on a line and, when it moves, the piece behind it falls.
examples: king left on the skewer file

concepts.means: Moving one piece uncovers an attack (or check) by another.
The move opened a file, rank or diagonal that lets an enemy piece reach a loose piece or the king.
examples: pawn capture opened a line to your knight
opened a diagonal to the king

concepts.means: A piece with no safe squares that can be won, or a piece that wandered off and got trapped.
An in-between move, desperado or capture first before retreating: the order of moves changes what is won.
Capturing, chasing or deflecting the opponent's defender so the thing it guarded falls.
Didn't see or answer what the opponent was threatening (other than mate), or didn't check the opponent's checks, captures and threats before moving.
examples: check every enemy check before moving
respond to the opponent's threat first

concepts.means: Missed or allowed a mating attack or pattern on the king (not specifically the back rank).
Back-rank mate or the threat of it: a king shut in behind its own pawns.
A king left in the centre, or losing the right to castle, while lines are opening.
Weakened the pawns or pieces sheltering the king: pawn moves in front of it, or giving up a key defender of its squares.
The king needs a flight square (luft) to avoid mate or endless checks.
examples: give the king an escape square

concepts.means: Allowed, or missed, a draw by perpetual check.
Stalemate as a resource or a trap.
Missed the chance to attack an exposed or weakened enemy king.
examples: open lines while king is in centre

concepts.means: Gaining time by attacking a piece (often with a pawn) so it must move, or putting a piece where it can be hit that way.
examples: bishop kicked by a pawn with tempo
retreat the queen with a threat

concepts.means: Wasted moves: one-move threats, chasing a piece to a better square, moving the same piece again.
examples: lost time with a one-move threat
chasing a piece to a better square

concepts.means: Developing pieces, or using or punishing a lead in development.
A pawn push that challenges or undermines the opponent's pawns and opens lines.
examples: undermine the b4 pawn with a5

concepts.means: Creating, pushing, stopping or blockading a passed pawn.
Creating or attacking weak pawns: isolated, backward, doubled or overextended.
Occupying or controlling the centre, with pawns or pieces.
Rooks on open files, the seventh rank, or behind passed pawns; a rook invading.
A piece on a poor square: knight on the rim, blocked bishop, piece where pawns can hit it, pieces blocking each other.
examples: don't put pieces where pawns can hit them

concepts.means: Controlling or taking away an important square or outpost.
examples: take d4 away from the knight

concepts.means: Whether to trade pieces: trade when ahead or defending, keep pieces when attacking, which piece to trade.
examples: trade queens to reach rook ending

concepts.means: Endgame know-how: which endings are drawn or won, king activity in the endgame, the opposition.
examples: activate your king in the endgame

concepts.means: None of the above fits. Keep the annotator's words as the text.
